https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.title: Brews (on the) up: the best teapots to buy now
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.text:
Gen Z are bringing the teapot back from the brink of extinction with a fresh enthusiasm for a brew. A quick dunk of a PG Tips teabag not good enough for them? Are they spending all their money on loose-leaf Darjeeling? A survey by Nationwide on the topic has failed to reveal the answers to these pressing questions.
What the survey of 2,000 does disclose is that more than half (59 per cent) of 16 to 28-year-olds have used a teapot in the past week, 74 per cent say tea is “essential to their lives” and that the Zoomers prefer tea over coffee, juice and energy drinks as the first drink of the day.
And there is more. As part of its Make Every Cuppa Count campaign last month, the charity Guide Dogs released a poll that named tea as the go-to drink for more than half of 18 to 24-year-olds, and traditional English breakfast tea as the most popular choice, followed by chai and green tea. The research also revealed that almost one in three had attended a tea party in the past year and 60 per cent of those surveyed expressed a desire to attend a tea party.
So which teapots are Gen Tea buying for these brew-based socials? Great British brands Burleigh and Cornishware have the market covered for street party style pots starting at £35 for a small blue and white striped Cornishware pot. Just add bunting and cake stands. The Cabbage pot at M&S, £18, and the pretty spriggy Annie, at Anthropologie, £36, have many fans but, across the stores, plain teapots are bestsellers. These often have a Japandi vibe, for instance Marimekko’s white porcelain Oiva, £79, and Ikea’s inexpensive Gladelig stoneware teapot, £15.
At David Mellor, the stainless-steel teapot, £95, is trending, possibly because of its high-profile appearances in stylish foodie hotspots. Cool customers for David Mellor classic pots include Gem Home (Flynn McGarry’s influential new venue in New York City) and Fedora (the new West Village restaurant by the people behind St Jardim). In London, Claire Ptak, the American baker who runs Violet Cakes’ Alaïa café on Bond Street uses David Mellor’s stainless teapots, as does Ochre, the National Gallery’s “bistro de luxe”.

Gone are the days of matchy-matchy tea sets, according to David Mellor’s James Lawless. “Customers aren’t really going for a teapot that’s part of a wider tableware set like they used to,” he says. “People might buy the tableware — plates, bowls etc — from a particular set or buy the teapot from the same set, but they rarely buy both. Teapots are definitely more of a standalone feature piece on the table. There’s history to this, though. Who doesn’t love a novelty teapot?”
Who indeed? The novelty teapot — the garden gnome of the kitchen table — is back in vogue. Visitors to Selfridges will encounter the surreal porcelain teapots of Seletti, an Italian brand that has created a vintage supermarket-inspired pop-up in the store. Meltdown, £130, appears to be dissolving in the heat.
Ceramic Inspirations, a maker in Leyburn, North Yorkshire, turns out eccentric pots in shapes from Colman’s Mustard tins to bathtubs and Marmite jars and posts them across the globe to a new and enthusiastic cohort of collectors (from £73). The Espresso machine teapot is a bestseller with the younger audience. To give an idea of the international interest in a kooky teapot, its Aga model comes in three styles: American (with waffles, muffins and a stars and stripes flag), Italian (including a pasta maker and olive oil) and British (choose from Sunday Lunch, Baking Day and English Breakfast, which features a tin of Teaz baked beans and ketchup bottle).
At the other end of the style spectrum lies the understated elegant glass teapot, favourite of the aficionados of herbal and flowering teas who shop at Newby Teas in London. A plain pot starts at £25. Stop by the shop during Clerkenwell Design Week, May 20-22, to see New Forms: Tea & Contemporary Design, an exhibition of handmade teapots including a graceful curving blue one by Jeremy Nichols, a sublime piece of salt glaze stoneware called Teapot 331, that will set you back £540.
The Zoomers are clearly onto something. It’s hard to see a downside to the teapot trend, which offers self-care, social activity and a cute accessory for the table. Maybe we all need to be more Gen Tea.
